articles.title: "I'm strictly d—ly" - Sophie Cunningham gets brutally honest about "lesbian mafia" in the WNBA
articles.summary: Theo Von asked Sophie Cunningham an unexpected question about the WNBA, and she had quite the answer.
articles.body:
Although people love her for her refreshing authenticity and confidence in who she is, Sophie Cunningham's natural beauty perfectly rounds out her unique character in modern sports, making her one of the most beloved athletes.

With her boldness, direct comments, and unapologetic personality that counter today's norms, the Indiana Fever guard has quickly gained a large fanbase, exceeding 4 million followers on Instagram.

What also makes Sophie different from most is her sexuality. Specifically, her preference is for males instead of females, as opposed to a significant number of WNBA players, who are gay.

Ultimately, everybody is aware of the unconventional dating scene in the WNBA.

Most notably, the league has seen a growing trend of players forming relationships with each other, whether on the same team or not, which has brought some hilarious drama on the court. Former lovers can become teammates, or current couple teammates can get traded away, etc.

"There is a web," said Sophie with a laugh on comedian Theo Von's podcast. "But it's, like, fascinating. I'm on the outside of that web. So, I just kind of sit back and eat my popcorn and watch it all unfold. And it's entertaining. It's fun."

On the flip side, having teammates date each other can become a high-risk scenario, as Michael Porter Jr. perfectly described .

So, when she was asked whether there is a "lesbian mafia" in the WNBA, Cunningham was quick to respond, reminding everyone of her sexual preference.

"Dude, honestly, I'm like strictly dickly. So I have no idea," said Sophie. "Like, I don't know who the mafia is or whatever."

"Like, guys only," said Sophie. "But like, to each their own. Go do what you want. I don't [care]. Like who gives a flying f–k."

And for the Fever guard, her only care in the world goes to how her team performs, regardless of anyone's relationship status.

Cunningham doesn't pay attention to the lore of former lovers

Still, there is some underlying lore that former lovers can get back at each other, such as flirting with an ex's teammate, as Von hilariously described. However, Sophie revealed she doesn't register those kinds of situations, as her only goal as an ultimate competitor is to get the W at the end of the day.

"I'm not in it, but you know your teammates and people they've been with or have not been with. You know the tea, what's going on. So, when you're playing those people, it's not like you're focused on that. You're literally trying to f–king win a game," said Cunningham.

For Sophie, she doesn't mind what goes on in other people's lives, as long as it doesn't affect her and the performance of her squad.

articles.title: Hezonja se aferra a la NBA
articles.standfirst: El alero exmadridista se hace un hueco en los Cavaliers y su regreso a Europa esta temporada parece descartado: en 10 días acaba el plazo para que pueda ser cortado
articles.summary: El alero exmadridista se hace un hueco en los Cavaliers y su regreso a Europa esta temporada parece descartado: en 10 días acaba el plazo para que pueda ser cortado
articles.body: Nada hace pensar que Mario Hezonja volverá a Europa esta misma temporada. Utilizar la cláusula de salida desde el Real Madrid hacia la NBA para después firmar un suculento contrato con otro equipo de Euroliga podía ser una opción, pero entre la advertencia de la Liga de que no lo hiciera y el rendimiento del alero croata eso se ha ido diluyendo. Cuando salió apresuradamente del club blanco en verano y firmó por los Cavaliers con un contrato mínimo de 2,8 millones de dólares se supo que ese acuerdo no estaba completamente garantizado. La franquicia tiene hasta el 15 de noviembre para ejecutar su corte. A 10 días de que expire el plazo, no parece realista que vaya a hacerlo. "Está la mentalidad y está el hambre. Puedo ayudar en muchas cosas, pero al final toda mi carrera en la NBA está en manos de Kenny [Atkinson, su entrenador], del cuerpo técnico y de mis compañeros. Todos han sido respetuosos conmigo y me hacer lucir como luzco en la cancha. Mi sincero agradecimiento de corazón va para ellos", dijo recientemente Porque Hezonja ha encajado como una pieza valiosa en la rotación de los Cavaliers y suele aprovechar sus minutos. Pese a ser el noveno que más juega del equipo (19,6), sus prestaciones son más que interesantes: 8,6 puntos, 5,9 rebotes, 2,0 asistencias, buen juego al poste aprovechando su superioridad física ante sus pares, sus clásicos lanzamientos a la media vuelta y un gran esfuerzo defensivo en los ocho encuentros que ha disputado hasta ahora en un conjunto que marcha 4-4 y no termina de arrancar pese a su gran potencial: Donovan Mitchell, James Harden, Evan Mobley, Jarret Allen... Han dolido especialmente las últimas dos derrotas consecutivas ante unos Thunder muy mermados por las lesiones. Al propio Hezonja se le pudo ver contrariado en el banquillo durante uno de los partidos, negando la cabeza y acabando con un "¡fuck!" (¡Joder!). Se topó en ocasiones con la defensa a Shai Gilgeous-Alexander y, pese a sus esfuerzos, el vigente MVP sumó 85 puntos entre las dos noches. Hezonja ha tenido que cambiar el chip de pasar de ser el referente absoluto en el ataque del Real Madrid a un secundario en los Cavaliers. En el equipo blanco lanzaba 12,1 tiros por partido en Liga Endesa y 11,4 en Euroliga. En la NBA se queda en 7,4. Es el octavo jugador de Cleveland que más lanza. No le queda más remedio que asumir ese nuevo rol y tratar de ganar algo más de protagonismo. Con 31 años y seis temporadas después de finalizar su primera etapa en la NBA, parece más maduro para encajar su nuevo hábitat. "Mi experiencia me relaja mucho. No me relaja competitivamente en la cancha, sino mentalmente", asegura. Antes de iniciar la temporada, el entrenador Atkinson ya mostró su satisfacción por disponer de un Hezonja muy mejorado en lo físico tras su etapa europea en el Panathinaikos, el UNICS y el Madrid. Comenzada la campaña ha alabado al croata en más de una ocasión: "Es un jugador con mucho talento para atacar, no quiero que se quede helado, metido en una caja. Lo quiero fuera, agresivo, haciendo jugadas y tirando en cuanto esté liberado". En eso anda el croata, intentando aprovechar cada oportunidad.

articles.title: La millonaria batalla de Londres por una franquicia en la NBA Europa afecta al Espanyol
articles.standfirst: La carrera por la franquicia de la NBA Europa en Londres se ha intensificado aún más en las últimas semanas
articles.summary: La carrera por la franquicia de la NBA Europa en Londres se ha intensificado aún más en las últimas semanas
articles.body: El diario 'The Sun' publica que Daniel Levy y Joe Lewis luchan por adquirir un equipo en Londres para competir en la "NBA Europa que empezará en 2027, haya o no acuerdo con la Euroliga". La relación entre el gestor Daniel Levy y multimillonario Joe Lewis es una histórica alianza de más de dos décadas vinculada al control del Tottenham Hotspur Football, que se rompió en 2025, y la firma de inversión ENIC Group. Jon Boon informa que la NBA tiene previsto invertir cerca de 9.100 millones de euros a lo largo de 10 años para poner en marcha su superliga europea de baloncesto, y que los expertos estiman que una franquicia con sede en Londres podría llegar a valer más de 1.197 millones de euros. Daniel Levy ha formado un consorcio con Liberty Global y MSP Sports Capital y han presentado una oferta. La familia Lewis forma parte de otro consorcio, liderado por la familia Checketts, que ha sido propietaria o ha invertido en entidades como el equipo de la MLS Real Salt Lake y los St. Louis Blues de la NHL. La familia Eccles, que posee participaciones en el Burnley FC y en el R.C.D. Espanyol, ha unido fuerzas con Lewis y los Checketts. 'Sky Sports' confirma que el triunvirato de familias presentó una oferta por el equipo de la NBA en Londres.

articles.title: Lorena Torres, la 'gurú' española de las Valkyries: el equipo de 1.000 millones que revoluciona la WNBA
articles.standfirst: La ibicenca Lorena Torres ha revolucionado el baloncesto femenino y la WNBA como como directora de rendimiento y del departamento médico de las Valkyries campeonas de la WNBA
articles.summary: La ibicenca Lorena Torres ha revolucionado el baloncesto femenino y la WNBA como como directora de rendimiento y del departamento médico de las Valkyries campeonas de la WNBA
articles.body: "Esto es lo que pasa cuando se invierte en deporte femenino". Fueron las palabras que pronunció la escolta Tiffany Hayes delante de las 18.064 personas que llenaron el pabellón Balhalla después de que las Golden State Valkyries levantasen el trofeo de campeonas de la WNBA el pasado sábado. Un hito histórico en el deporte de Estados Unidos, ya que la franquicia se creó hace apenas dos temporadas fichando a las jugadoras prescindibles de otros equipos y, ahora, todo lo que tocan estas Valkyries lo convierten en oro. Hace unos meses, fueron la primera franquicia de la WNBA en estar valorada en 1.000 millones de dólares, según medios estadounidenses. Además, han agotado las entradas en todos los partidos que han jugado como locales durante sus dos años de existencia, llenando el Chase Center, rebautizado como Ballhala cuando juegan ellas. Precisamente, el séptimo partido de las finales ante las Atlanta Dream ha sido el más visto en la historia de los 'playoffs' de la WNBA, congregando a más de 3,3 millones de espectadores por televisión. Todo un récord en los 30 años de vida que tiene la liga. "Resuelven cada detalle para que tú lo único que tengas que hacer es preocuparte de jugar al baloncesto", dijo la 'Jugadora Mejor Valorada' (MVP) de las finales Gabby Williams sobre la forma de trabajo de la franquicia. La alero franco-estadounidense firmó una actuación antológica en el partido decisivo con 28 puntos en la segunda mitad ante las Dream. En el momento más importante de la temporada, apareció la mejor Gabby y una de las responsables de eso fue la española Lorena Torres, la directora de rendimiento y del departamento médico de las Valkyries. "En las entrevistas de fin de temporada, analizando individualmente cómo había ido, Gabby me dio las gracias porque me dijo: 'me ha ido súper bien la gestión de minutos, me he sentido bien cuando me he tenido que sentir bien'", explicó la ibicenca a EFE. Torres es la máxima responsable en la toma de decisiones deportivas como, por ejemplo, la duración y la intensidad de los entrenamientos o los procesos de recuperación de las jugadoras. "Todo el mundo ha creído en la estrategia. Estoy feliz de haber podido ayudar a esta jugadora, que es la estrella, y a otras del equipo a que rindieran a su máximo nivel cuando tenían que hacerlo", afirmó. La irrupción de estas Valkyries, con un juego colectivo, en equipo y sin grandes 'superestrellas' en su plantilla, ha supuesto todo un terremoto en el baloncesto femenino estadounidense, que suele tender a un juego más individualista y centrado en las grandes jugadoras. El conjunto de Natalie Nakase, con este éxito colectivo, ha redefinido el estándar de la liga y puede ser el comienzo de una nueva era. "Es complejo que la gente entienda lo que hemos conseguido. Al ser un equipo en expansión, no tienes acceso a superestrellas porque el sistema es el que es. Los equipos intentan tener el 'Big 3' y nosotras teníamos que pensar otra estrategia. Diseñamos una plantilla en la que tuviésemos banquillo y eso nos ha permitido toda la temporada gestionar los minutos de juego de las jugadoras, porque sabíamos que cuando el banquillo empezase a jugar nos iban a aguantar el marcador", reflexionó la española. Esta ha sido una de las claves del éxito sobre el parqué de la franquicia de San Francisco. La francesa Janelle Salaün ha sido seleccionada como la 'Mejor Sexta Jugadora' de la temporada, aportando 12,7 puntos desde el banco. Y este reconocimiento no es casualidad porque, como reconoce la propia Torres, tras su paso por la selección española o franquicias de la NBA como los Spurs o los Sixers a lo largo de su trayectoria. "El sexto y séptimo hombre son clave. Eso se lo dije a la General Manager. Creo que es un estilo más europeo, diferente y, en este año, ha funcionado. Puede que la próxima temporada tengamos tres superestrellas y me tocará gestionar ese contexto", concluyó. En una entrevista con EFE Lorena Torres repasa su trayectoria y explica cómo convirtió el reto de construir una franquicia desde cero en un éxito histórico. Apenas dos temporadas de existencia de la franquicia y ya han ganado el anillo. ¿Son conscientes de la dimensión de lo que han conseguido? Ha sido muy emocionante. Ayer de reuniones estábamos todos diciendo: ¿es real? ¿lo hemos conseguido? Estamos un poco en 'shock'. Hemos ido partido a partido y hemos ganado, aunque era el objetivo, sigue siendo como ¡guau!. Hemos llenado el pabellón de los Warriors (NBA) todos los partidos con nuestros propios fans. Los fans de los Warriors y los nuestros no son los mismos, pero el deporte es espectáculo y si lo das, hay espacio para todos. Se siente como estar en el sitio adecuado, en el momento oportuno. ¿Cómo se ha vivido este éxito desde dentro? Con mucha emoción, mucha alegría. La gente no es consciente de lo duro que ha sido, del poco tiempo que hemos tenido para ganar un anillo. El partido empezó cómo queríamos porque si Atlanta se ponía a meter triples luego es muy difícil pararles. Los últimos 45 segundos de partido estaba mirando al suelo, no quería ver lo que pasaba, pero levanté la cabeza y vi que todo el mundo estaba con el confeti, saltando… Cuando le dan la oportunidad de crear desde cero el departamento de rendimiento. ¿Cómo lo afronta? ¿Cómo se consigue ganar el campeonato de la WNBA en apenas dos temporadas? En 2024 esta franquicia no existía. El año pasado fue un poco de supervivencia, queríamos meternos en 'playoffs'. Me centré en montar un equipo de trabajo, un staff, los procesos, cómo iban a ser nuestros calentamientos… Estábamos construyendo todo, mientras que el cuerpo técnico estaba enfocado en ganar partidos. Pero en post-temporada, cuando tuvimos tiempo de analizar cómo iba la temporada, la General Manager, la entrenadora y yo, que somos el triángulo de mujeres que tomamos todas las decisiones deportivas, decidimos hacer una estrategia para llegar en nuestro mejor pico de forma a los 'playoffs', con el objetivo de ganar. Mi parte fue diseñar una estrategia para que durante toda la temporada pudiéramos mantener a las jugadoras lo más sanas posibles. Yo era la responsable de decir cómo se entrena y cómo se descansa, la duración de los entrenamientos, la intensidad, etc. Y tener banquillo nos ha permitido toda la temporada gestionar los minutos de juego de las jugadoras. La estrategia de carga-recuperación y el 'feedback' constante con las jugadoras nos ha ayudado mucho a lo hemos conseguido. A lo largo de su carrera ha formado parte de muchos equipos ganadores, como la selección española masculina, los San Antonio Spurs o los Philadelphia 76ers de la NBA, pero ¿qué tiene de diferente esta franquicia respecto a las otras en las que ha trabajado? Lo más diferente es que siempre he ido a sitios en los que el sistema ya estaba y tú llegabas a aportar tu experiencia, tu conocimiento. Montarlo todo desde cero ha sido distinto y muy bonito porque tenía carta blanca para hacer lo que quisiera. También ha sido diferente la colaboración. Nunca había estado en un sitio en el que yo he tenido tanto peso en la toma de decisión, en la estrategia, en mi rol. Para mí ha sido única la colaboración y la comunicación entre la General Manager, entrenadora y la persona que se encarga del rendimiento y la salud (ella). Ha sido espectacular. Como franquicia, el segundo año he visto que en esta franquicia, si creen en ti, te ayudan muchísimo. Que crean en ti, te respeten y te apoyen, eso eleva muchísimo el rendimiento. Para mí personalmente, trabajar en un ambiente de mujeres. He trabajado muchos años en ambientes de hombres y es distinto. Ha sido un ambiente muy sano, queremos tener buena gente, formar parte de la construcción de una cultura tan sana en el ambiente profesional, que muchas veces es muy tóxico. ¿Cree que el crecimiento de la WNBA está contribuyendo también a impulsar la investigación y el conocimiento sobre la salud de la mujer deportista? Estamos viviendo un momento en la historia del deporte, donde la mujer tiene su espacio. Y se está apostando por la mujer, conocer a la mujer, hacer investigación, al menos aquí en Estados Unidos. Muchas veces tenemos como referencia estudios masculinos y hay pocos de mujeres, que además son de poca calidad. En los últimos dos meses me han contactado los dos grupos de investigación deportiva más potentes del mundo, porque las mujeres quieren saber más sobre la mujer y cómo ayudar a la mujer, con parámetros femeninos. Dijo el otro día que lo que en España se ve como un gasto, en Estados Unidos es una inversión. ¿Qué diferencias destacaría desde su experiencia entre la forma en que Estados Unidos y España entienden, valoran y apuestan por el deporte? El deporte en España es deficitario y esto me cuesta mucho entenderlo. Aquí es un negocio y es un negocio que va muy bien. Es un tema cultural, el deporte está constantemente en la televisión, deporte de hombres, mujeres, universitario… El fan está expuesto al deporte mucho tiempo. En España es deficitario y aquí da muchísimo dinero, ¿cómo puede ser? ¿Qué no estamos haciendo en España y en Europa para que no dé tanto dinero como da aquí? El tema de patrocinadores e inversión es distinto en España. Aquí tienes dinero de 'ticketing', de 'merchandinsing', además de patrocinadores que invierten muchísimo dinero. Claro que puedes tener mejores resultados si inviertes, la gente lo que le tiene que dar una vuelta es a cómo conseguir recursos. Es el mismo deporte, pero en dos partes del mundo. No es solo tener tecnología, también hay que invertir en personal y la gente buena quiere cobrar bien. Es un tema de inversión de arriba a abajo: sueldos, equipamiento, colaboraciones con investigación, publicidad, marketing, etc. Es muy distinto. Con recursos y con talento, de los jugadores, del staff, de la gente que toma decisiones, se puede ganar. Eso es lo bonito de WNBA, que es muy difícil que un equipo gane dos veces seguidas, en España tenemos 3 equipos que ganan siempre. Es un tema complejo.

articles.title: LeBron James took a risk going to the 76ers this offseason. So far, it’s paying off.
articles.summary: James, who switched teams for the fourth time in free agency over the summer, has helped lead the Philadelphia 76ers to the hottest start in the NBA.
articles.body: When his agent, Rich Paul, revealed on a whiteboard the teams likeliest to sign him in the summer, LeBron James appeared to be choosing among five contenders after he entered free agency: the Philadelphia 76ers, the Miami Heat, the Minnesota Timberwolves, the Denver Nuggets and the Cleveland Cavaliers. James, in something of a surprise, picked the 76ers. And through the (very) early part of this season, he appears to have chosen wisely. Philadelphia is 8-1 after a win over the Detroit Pistons on Wednesday night. The 76ers have the most wins in the NBA entering Friday, and their high-powered starting five has jelled quickly to form an undeniable title contender. The starting five In addition to signing James, Philly traded for swingman Jaylen Brown in the offseason, forming a starting five of James, Brown, Tyrese Maxey, V.J. Edgecombe and Joel Embiid. Those five players have combined for 36 All-Star selections, five MVP awards and five Finals MVP awards. So it’s perhaps unsurprising the group has been great together on the floor. In 77 minutes together across five games, the Sixers’ starting five has outscored opponents by 15 points. Philadelphia’s opening quintet is dominating defensively, holding opponents to only 95.4 points per 100 possessions. (For context, the league’s best defense entering Thursday was holding opponents to 103 points per 100 possessions.) “Our defense is going to be our identity,” James said Wednesday after the win over the Pistons. “We have a lot of scoring. We know that from individuals. We’re still figuring out that side of the floor out on the offensive side. Defensively, that’s where we are going to make our mark.” James has meshed well with all of his co-stars so far. All two-man lineups featuring a combo of James plus one of Maxey, Brown, Embiid and Edgecombe have outscored opponents through the team’s first nine games. James is clearly pacing himself Playing on a roster loaded with talent, James has seemingly been happy to become one of the best role players in the NBA. Through his first seven games, James is averaging 15.7 points, 7.4 rebounds and 7.4 assists a night. His scoring average, field-goal attempts per game (13.1) and free-throw attempts (4.4) are all on pace to be career-low marks. While James hasn’t necessarily made up for the dip in efficiency — his 45.7% shooting from the field would be his lowest since his rookie season — his willingness to take a back seat has helped Maxey in particular. The speedy guard is averaging 28.0 points on a career-best 48.6% shooting. “It was a long offseason for me,” Maxey said this month. “I worked on my passing. I worked on my isolation scoring and my late-game scoring. I wanted to be able to come back with a move that I could get to late in games, because I knew we were going to need it. I knew we would need it, and I knew that I would be ready to do it.” Said Brown: “Max has been leading the way, 100%. He’s been here. This is his team.” Everyone has sacrificed to some degree, including Embiid, who admitted he was struggling adapting to his new role as his shot attempts diminish. “My mindset is really on whenever I have the ball, make plays,” Embiid said. “Make the game easy for all these guys. Making the right play over and over, setting screens, get Tyrese as open as possible, Bron, all these guys.” How does this compare to previous James teams? Typically, when James joins a new team, it takes a little while for things to come together. The 2010-11 Miami Heat, for example, started only 6-4 in their first 10 games. The team was only 9-8 after 17 games, when James famously bumped into coach Erik Spoelstra during the team’s eighth loss. The 2014-15 Cleveland Cavaliers were worse, starting 5-5 when James returned home. The Cavs struggled until January, hovering around .500 until they embarked on a 12-game winning streak midseason. The 2018-19 Los Angeles Lakers started the season 4-6 and eventually missed the playoffs after James sustained a groin injury late in the year. Much of that team was turned over the following offseason after the Lakers acquired Anthony Davis. This year’s 76ers have a chance to go 9-1 if they win Friday. And history already bodes well for Philly, as the four previous James-led teams to start 7-1 all made the NBA Finals. “It’s too early to be talking about the Finals and things of that nature on Nov. 4,” James said Wednesday night. “We got a good team. Guys vibe with one another, guys like each other, guys enjoy being around each other.”

articles.title: NBA Power Rankings with LeBron James' 76ers, Victor Wembanyama's Spurs Rising
articles.summary: Now over two weeks into the 2026-27 NBA campaign, we have enough games to start rolling out more informed takes.
articles.body:
Now over two weeks into the 2026-27 NBA campaign, we have enough games to start rolling out more informed takes.

The Philadelphia 76ers are no longer just a theoretical juggernaut. Calling Luka Dončić's start MVP worthy doesn't do it justice. Victor Wembanyama is starting to look like Wilt Chamberlain. And that barely scratches the surface of what we saw this week.

With every team's recent performance in mind, and based on team and individual numbers, championship chances and plenty of subjectivity, here's how the entire league stacks up right now.

ATL | BKN | BOS | CHA | CHI | CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GSW | HOU | IND | LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN | NOP | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX | POR | SAC | SAS | TOR | UTA | WAS

The Chicago Bulls are now the sole owners of the worst net rating in the NBA (by a pretty wide margin). And their biggest source of hope is really struggling to adjust to NBA defenses.

Caleb Wilson leads the Bulls in scoring at 19.5 points per game, but he's shooting just 40.9 percent from the field. After going 2-of-12 in Wednesday's loss, he's been under 50 percent in six of his eight games.

Most rookies go through some growing pains, but those numbers are a little alarming. In coming weeks, Wilson may need to cut down a bit on his off-the-dribble attempts, and Chicago's playmakers need to create some easier looks for him.

The Sacramento Kings are going to be one of the worst teams in the NBA this season. They should be aggressively pursuing trades to unload Domantas Sabonis and Zach LaVine.

Those are the obvious and not-so-fun aspects of this season that would typically drive fans away.

But this team also has one of the most entertaining players in the league in rookie guard Darius Acuff, whose aggression in hunting his own shot is early 2000s-esque, and yet somehow not off-putting.

Acuff is averaging 25.6 points on 23.6 attempts, but it's not like there are a ton of significantly better scoring options on the roster. And in his last four games, Acuff is also putting up 9.3 assists.

On paper, the Milwaukee Bucks have a handful of talented players who should at least make this team scrappy (like they were in Wednesday's matchup with the Boston Celtics, when they erased a 22-point deficit before eventually losing), but they don't have a clear alpha.

And outside of a few stretches here and there, the talent hasn't coalesced for winning basketball.

Still, players like Tyler Herro (22.3 points, 3.9 assists and a 42.6 three-point percentage) and Jaime Jaquez (16.8 points, 6.6 rebounds and 2.8 assists in 28.5 minutes) are at least establishing a little trade value in the event Milwaukee chases more assets for the post-Giannis era.

In the year the Utah Jazz were supposed to turn the corner and start winning games again, Jaren Jackson Jr. was lost after four games for 6-8 weeks with a torn MCL, Darryn Peterson has lagged behind his draft-class peers and Jusuf Nurkić has yet to appear in a game.

And the Jazz, perhaps unsurprisingly, have not been able to live up to lofty preseason expectations.

On the bright side, aside from ho-hum scoring efficiency, Keyonte George (22.0 points and 5.9 assists) is following up his 2025-26 breakout well. And while Peterson is shooting just 35.4 percent from the field, his 3.8 assists in 30.3 minutes per game suggests he may be ready for real playmaking duties earlier than expected.

The Los Angeles Clippers nearly secured an overtime win over the Miami Heat on Wednesday, but Klay Thompson's buzzer-beating three gave them their third straight loss.

And with each passing week, it gets harder to find reasons for optimism.

L.A. doesn't have its own pick this summer, and that's not even the result of the punishment for circumventing the salary cap (the Clippers are still paying off the Paul George trade). Rookie Keaton Wagler is shooting 30.9 percent from the field. And there's no firm return timetable for their potential leading scorer, Brandon Ingram.

Darius Garland (20.9 points and 6.6 assists) is having a solid campaign, but he's not the kind of player who can singlehandedly lift a roster this shallow.

The Brooklyn Nets had a solid little 2-2 week to separate themselves from the dregs of the net rating column.

Michael Porter Jr. (21.4 points and 7.4 rebounds, with a 38.9 three-point percentage) and Julius Randle (21.0 points, 7.1 rebounds and 4.8 assists) have been the obvious factors for mild competitiveness, but they had some young help in Wednesday's win over the Charlotte Hornets.

Danny Wolf made his third appearance of the season, totaled 12 points, five rebounds and three assists in that contest and moved his season long plus-minus to plus-26.

He also looked like exactly the kind of skilled big who could create a bit and take some pressure off MPJ and Randle on offense.

The Charlotte Hornets went 0-4 since the last edition of the power rankings dropped, and that's not even the worst news of the week.

Kon Knueppel made his season debut on Wednesday, but he had to leave after just six minutes due to soreness in the leg that kept him out till this point of the season.

In 2025-26, Charlotte's net rating, offensive rating, effective field-goal percentage and turnover percentage all improved when Knueppel was on the floor. And if this season's net rating is any indication, his impact as a shooter and secondary creator is sorely missed.

They do get a bit of a pass with Paolo Banchero being out for their last six games, but it's probably past time to worry about the Orlando Magic in a more general sense.

Beyond falling to 2-6 after a blowout loss to the uninspiring Phoenix Suns on Thursday, the Banchero-Franz Wagner pairing has never totally worked. There's almost too much overlap in their games, and a plus-1.5 net rating over the duo's four-plus seasons together doesn't scream contender.

If the Magic don't turn things around quickly and dramatically whenever Banchero does return (ideally, in late November), one or both forwards could become the most intriguing trade candidates in the NBA.

The Phoenix Suns were in dire need of a win on Thursday, so it's a good thing the reeling Orlando Magic came to town.

And on closer examination of their schedule, the Suns' tough start may not be as bad as the raw wins and losses suggest.

Every team Phoenix has lost to is above .500 right now. It's only victory was over a winning team too.

There are real concerns about the shot selection of Jalen Green and defensive shortcomings of Green, Devin Booker and Miles Bridges. Mark Williams being out has put a spotlight on the lack of depth at the 5.

But it's OK to withhold judgment on this mix till we see it get a few more opportunities against teams like Orlando.

The Miami Heat need a Klay Thompson buzzer beater in overtime to sneak past the woeful Los Angeles Clippers on Wednesday. The next night, they got run out of the gym by the shorthanded Golden State Warriors.

And although we're less than a month into this campaign, Heat fans have to be hovering a finger around the panic button.

The offense is ho-hum, largely because the two best players (Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo) don't really fit together. And that's not even the biggest problem.

A team that was supposed to be dominant defensively, with Giannis, Bam and Davion Mitchell, is getting lit up to the tune of 117.7 points per 100 possessions (a defensive rating that puts Miami in the bottom five).

The good vibes generated by Tyrese Haliburton's return were short-lived, as he's now missed the last five games with a hamstring strain and the Indiana Pacers went through a five-game losing streak that actually started before Haliburton went down.

The good news is that Indiana beat the red-hot Memphis Grizzlies on the road to close this week. And Pascal Siakam (21.8 points, 7.1 rebounds and 3.8 assists) and Andrew Nembhard (19.0 points and 6.9 assists) are both playing well.

When Haliburton returns (the original timeline, which started in late October, was at least two weeks), the Pacers should be able to get back on track.

The Washington Wizards will clearly be better than last season's team (really, the last several seasons'), but comfortably making the playoffs will require much better shooting.

The roster is shooting just 29.4 percent from deep, and the numbers are no better for the leaders than they are for the role players. Trae Young, Anthony Davis and AJ Dybantsa's combined three-point percentage is 29.1.

At the very least, Young and Dybantsa should be better. If they're not, defenses will be able to sag off their on-ball opportunities, crowd the paint and make offense a chore for the Wizards.

Last week's New Orleans Pelicans blurb started by declaring them to be "better than their record suggests," and they backed me up on that this week.

After starting the season 0-4, New Orleans is back to .500, with two of the wins in the current streak coming against quality opponents (the Atlanta Hawks and Memphis Grizzlies).

They got back on track with a balanced attack that includes Zion Williamson (21.5 points and 2.5 steals), Dejounte Murray (18.2 points and 5.6 assists), Trey Murphy III (14.9 points), Jeremiah Fears (13.6 points and 4.5 assists) and Derik Queen (13.4 points and 3.0 assists), but the real X-factor may be Saddiq Bey.

In just 26.6 minutes per game, Bey is averaging 16.4 points and 1.8 threes.

Cooper Flagg and the Dallas Mavericks returned to earth a bit this week.

After averaging 26.8 points and shooting 55.7 percent from the field in his first five games, Flagg put up 18.0 and shot 26.3 percent over his last two (both losses).

But it'd be silly to put too much stock into two off nights from a 19-year-old, especially when Dallas is still plus-8.1 points per 100 possessions when he shares the floor with Kyrie Irving.

Life without Kawhi Leonard has proven difficult for the Toronto Raptors.

After a blowout loss to the Denver Nuggets on Wednesday, Toronto is now 2-4 without Kawhi. And surprisingly, it's the defense that's letting them down.

The Raptors, despite rankings 25th in three-point percentage, have a top-seven offense thanks to Scottie Barnes' and RJ Barrett's slashing and team-wide dominance of the offensive glass. But in their four losses, they're giving up 124.3 points per game.

Jalen Johnson has been banged up, and the Atlanta Hawks' offense has been uninspiring, but Nickeil Alexander-Walker has more than backed up last season's breakout and has this team over .500.

After going for 26 in Atlanta's win over the Washington Wizards on Wednesday, Alexander-Walker is up to 21.7 points in 30.5 minutes, while shooting 40.7 percent from deep this season.

When Johnson rejoins him in the rotation full time, and if Kingston Flemings continues to look more NBA-ready than expected (he had 14 points in his first career start on Wednesday), the Hawks should be able to stay in the mix for a top-six finish throughout the season.

The Cleveland Cavaliers' offense is generally fine. Donovan Mitchell (22.5 points and 5.5 assists, with a 41.1 three-point percentage) and Evan Mobley (18.8 points and 3.5 assists, with a 48.6 three-point percentage) are playing well on that end, and the team is ninth in points per 100 possessions.

But Cleveland is still among the more disappointing teams in the league in this early portion of the season, thanks to a bottom-10 defense that may be getting worse.

Perhaps their two best defenders, Peyton Watson (hamstring) and Jarrett Allen (knee) are dealing with minor injuries that could keep them out (or at least slow them down) for the next few games.

The Denver Nuggets' 23rd -ranked defense figures to be a problem throughout this season, but there are reasons for optimism.

Nikola Jokić, despite a slow-by-his-standards start, is averaging 23.4 points, 9.7 rebounds, 9.3 assists, 2.1 steals and 1.1 blocks. Jamal Murray is putting up 25.4 points, while shooting 50.9 percent from deep. And Trevon Brazile, Bryce Hopkins and Marvin Bagley have infused more energy into the second unit than this team has had in years.

Jokić's scoring efficiency is still well below his career norms, and he has to offer at least some resistance on defense, but the foundation of a 50-win team is still in place.

The Golden State Warriors have now rattled off six straight wins, and Stephen Curry and Yaxel Lendeborg suddenly look like one of the most dynamic duos in the entire NBA.

In Thursday's blowout win over the Miami Heat, Curry hit six threes and tallied 29 points, bringing his average to 29.9. Lendeborg added 17 points, eight rebounds, six assists and three steals, bringing his well-rounded averages to 21.0 points, 7.1 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 1.1 steals.

The team is somehow losing the minutes when both are on the floor, but it's hard to imagine that lasting with the way both are producing and with how well their games mesh. Lendeborg's slashing is an ideal complement to Curry's shooting, which in turn pulls attention away from those Lendeborg drives.

The Memphis Grizzlies lost their last two games, but their combined deficit in those contests was five points. And their net rating actually went up this week.

Yes, four of their six wins have come against the Utah Jazz and Sacramento Kings, but the foundation of a good team is clearly in place here.

Ty Jerome (27.4 points and 5.3 assists), Cameron Boozer (16.5 points, 9.8 rebounds and 5.4 assists) and Cedric Coward (14.3 points, 8.7 rebounds and a 50.0 three-point percentage) are all winning players. And there's enough depth in place to survive random absences from any of the above.

The Oklahoma City deserve a mountain of credit for their resilience over the last two seasons.

Despite almost constant injury struggles, OKC just keeps winning.

And while role players like Ajay Mitchell (17.8 points and 3.5 assists), Aday Mara (6.8 points, 5.5 rebounds and 1.9 blocks in 19.0 minutes) and Bennett Stirtz (12.0 points per game over his last three) deserve plenty of credit, it's obviously Shai Gilgeous-Alexander who's carrying them.

In the five games since Jalen Williams, Cason Wallace and Chet Holmgren all went down, SGA is putting up 31.6 points and 4.8 assists, while shooting 38.9 percent from deep. And he's gotten to at least 42 points and 12 free-throw attempts in each of his last two outings.

The Portland Trail Blazers may not be ready to join the contenders' tier just yet, but it's getting harder and harder to deny their status as an obvious playoff team.

Deni Avdija's (23.4 points, 6.4 assists and 6.3 rebounds) slashing has looked like a perfect complement to Damian Lillard's (20.1 points and 4.1 assists) shooting, and neither is above 32 percent from deep. If one or both start hitting threes, Portland could look even better.

But the real key to their success may be the three-and-D role playing of Toumani Camara (47.1 percent from deep), Jrue Holiday (42.5 percent) and Donovan Clingan (46.7 percent).

The Detroit Pistons ended their week with a loss to the Philadelphia 76ers, but things are clearly looking, in spite of the absence of Jalen Duren for all but two games.

Cade Cunningham (24.0 points and 7.6 assists) is the most obvious reason why, but Duncan Robinson deserves a spotlight too.

In his age-32 season, Robinson is averaging a career-high (by far) 19.0 points, while shooting 47.9 percent from deep.

For a team that relies so heavily on defense, size and scoring inside, Robinson's gravity as an off-ball mover and catch-and-shoot threat has been vital.

After starting their 2026-27 campaign with three straight losses, the New York Knicks have worked their way back to .500.

And Jalen Brunson (25.6 points and 5.1 assists) and Karl-Anthony Towns (19.9 points and 13.6 rebounds in 31.2 minutes, while shooting 42.9 percent from three) are both looking like the superstars who led the Knicks to the title just five months ago.

But there's still some cause for mild concern. New York's bench, with the exception of Landry Shamet, isn't producing much. And Mikal Bridges is averaging just 6.3 points on 7.1 shots per game.

The Minnesota Timberwolves dropped eight spots in last week's power rankings, mostly due to the anticipated absence of Anthony Edwards, who's out for a couple months after an arthroscopic knee surgery.

As it turns out, that was too pessimistic a view of Edwards' supporting cast, who've gone 3-2 since Edwards left the rotation, just closed out this week with a win over the Houston Rockets and now have the best net rating in the league.

The surge is due to stout defense and a balanced attack from Ayo Dosunmu (19.8 points and 4.6 assists), LaMelo Ball (19.2 points, 5.6 assists and 39.1 three-point percentage), Jaden McDaniels (17.6 points and 4.2 assists), Jonathan Kuminga (13.6 points and 3.2 assists, with a 46.2 three-point percentage) and Bones Hyland (13.4 points and 4.2 assists, with a 41.4 three-point percentage).

Even in today's high-paced and high-volume-three-point-shooting era, with officiating that heavily favors offenses, Luka Dončić's offensive numbers are almost unfathomable.

After another 40-point outing on Wednesday, Luka is averaging 38.5 points, 8.1 rebounds, 8.0 assists and a would-be- record 5.9 threes.

And while it's fair to wonder if Luka's heliocentric dominance will translate to playoff success, there's no question it's leading to wins now.

On the season, the Los Angeles Lakers are plus-20.1 points per 100 possessions with Dončić on the floor and minus-15.4 when he's off.

Things aren't perfect for the Boston Celtics. They got walloped by the Houston Rockets this week. And their three-point accuracy (12th in percentage) and volume (10th in makes per game) aren't as moving as they've been in the past.

But the Celtics and their fans can take solace in at least this: The Paul George and Jayson Tatum duo is working.

Tatum is putting up 27.0 points and 7.9 assists, while George is at 21.3 points and 5.0 assists with a 41.4 three-point percentage. And both have looked capable of carrying the offense while the other is off the floor.

The Houston Rockets cooled off this week, going 2-2 and losing a game to the Anthony Edwards-less Minnesota Timberwolves, but they still look like one of the deepest, most well-rounded teams in the NBA.

Houston has seven players averaging double-figures (with Marcus Smart nearly there at 9.8 points). It has six players averaging at least 2.5 assists. It has Kevin Durant to get tough buckets when the offense bogs down. And it has a fringe MVP candidate in Alperen Şengün.

The Rockets' star center is averaging 22.4 points, 9.1 rebounds, 8.1 assists, 1.3 steals and 1.1 blocks.

Right when it looked like Luka Dončić might completely run away with the MVP race, Victor Wembanyama had a single-game performance the likes of which we haven't seen since the 1960s .

In Wednesday's win over the Dallas Mavericks, Wemby totaled an eye-popping 52 points, 24 rebounds, eight blocks, two steals and, for good measure, two assists. And he packed all of that into 34 minutes.

Even at 22 years old, a night like this one is clear evidence that Wembanyama is already in the "best in the world" mix. And with 20-year-old Dylan Harper having his own breakout with 18.6 points and 4.6 assists, the Spurs have a real argument to be No. 1 here.

It's still early, and six of their eight victories have been by single digits, but the Philadelphia 76ers are bucking a trend that's hovered around the NBA for nearly two decades.

The last superteam that was largely assembled in one offseason and came together this quickly was the 2007-08 Boston Celtics (the 2016-17 Golden State Warriors were already a superteam before Kevin Durant joined).

And the similarities between that team and this one are obvious. Boston won with defense. Philly is top three on that end. Ray Allen and Kevin Garnett made sacrifices and deferred to Paul Pierce to make the offense work. Jaylen Brown, Joel Embiid and LeBron James are doing the same with Tyrese Maxey.

And the further we get into this season, the easier it is to imagine the Sixers ending the season the same way the 2008 Celtics did; raising a trophy.

articles.title: Ranking the Top 10 Women's College Basketball Players Early in 2026-27
articles.summary: The NCAA women's basketball season is upon us.
articles.body:
The NCAA women's basketball season is upon us.

Many players can help their programs make deep runs and reach the heights they have spent all summer working for, but some stars stand above the crowd.

These are the top 10 NCAA women's basketball players early in the 2026-2027 season.

Michigan has been on a steady climb over the last couple of years. Olivia Olson has largely led the charge. The season didn't end the way Olson would have wanted, as Michigan suffered a blowout loss to Texas in the NCAA tournament, but that loss can be a lesson.

The key piece to Olson's game taking the next step will be getting her three-point percentage back up after shooting 38.3% from deep in her freshman season, but dropping to 30.5% last year.

In terms of production and caliber of opponent compared to the discussion of an individual player, Ohio State's Jaloni Cambridge might be the most underrated player in the nation.

Averaging 23.2 points per game last season, the offensive electricity that she brings powers Ohio State in many ways. This is another season where she'll look to do so and potentially break containment, joining the larger national conversation at a higher level. Don't be surprised if you see her in the running for Big Ten Player of the Year.

As the lone true center on this list, Clara Strack is the anchor of everything for Kentucky. Averaging a double-double last season with 16.9 PPG and 10.1 RPG, expectations are high for what Strack can do this year in the SEC.

It feels like there is more untapped potential in terms of true game-takeover potential on the offensive end; if Kentucky head coach Kenny Brooks can find a way to get to it consistently, you can see Strack rise up this list and WNBA Draft boards. She has the touch offensively while being a direct deterrent at the rim for opposing teams. There is a whole lot to like from Strack's game.

Unrivaled Power Rankings After Full 2027 Roster Release

When JuJu Watkins went down, there were understandable questions about how USC would fill the void the following season. Jazzy Davidson took that challenge head-on and impressed in her freshman campaign.

It wasn't without some growing pains, but Davidson was immensely impactful on both sides of the ball. She was asked to do it all as the stat sheets kept filling up.

After averaging 17.9 points and two steals and blocks per game, it will be an adjustment for the reigning National Freshman of the Year as Watkins returns. If USC can figure it out, they can be the best duo in the country.

6. Joyce Edwards, South Carolina, Forward

Unsurprisingly, South Carolina is once again stacked with talent, but Joyce Edwards will lead the way this season. Last year, Edwards was tasked with a large increase in responsibility due to the Gamecocks having some of their depth unavailable. Edwards took that increase in stride.

Starting every game and upping her scoring average to 19.2 points per game, she enters this season with that growth and reinforcements that should make her life easier in the paint. With Dawn Staley and her staff's track record of developing bigs, don't be surprised if Edwards takes another leap.

When you are a 3x First Team All-American, a former Big 12 and SEC Player of the Year, it is hard to imagine having more to prove. Yet Madison Booker might be the player with the most opportunity to cement their dominance on this list.

Booker has one of the most unstoppable jump shots in the game with her pull-up in the mid-range. It has guided Texas to back-to-back NCAA Final Four appearances. As she enters her senior year after an off-season of roster turnover for Texas, her ability to lead this team deep once again and the potential growth of her three-point shot will be the things to watch to see her leap up this list.

For the longest time, the SEC has been run by bigs dominating in the paint, using their size to assert their command. Then Vanderbilt's Mikayla Blakes came along. With a nation-leading 27 points per game last season, she has Vandy ready to reach for the greatest of heights.

Blakes has carried a ton of responsibility over her first two years in the NCAA, but she has taken it in stride. Whether it is her using her speed to get to the rim, getting to the free-throw line, or knocking down a three, the defense is in trouble if Blakes has the ball.

If you look up "dawg mentality" in the dictionary, there are no words. It's just a picture of Notre Dame's Hannah Hidalgo. Few players have the talent of a superstar but the mentality of someone fighting for their roster spot. You mix that with the supreme athleticism that Hidalgo possesses, and you have a player who is one of one.

You can say a lot about Hidalgo's ability to attack offensively, where she averaged 25.3 PPG, but nothing is more impressive than her ability to force turnovers defensively. She averaged an unfathomable 5.6 steals per game, highlighted by her Sweet 16 matchup against Vanderbilt, where she tallied 10 steals and was only three assists off from a quadruple-double. The moment the opposing team gets the ball, they are simply in danger. This gives Hidalgo a unique ability to take over games.

She is back. The last time we saw JuJu Watkins play a full season, she dominated and was on the cusp of a potential deep run toward the NCAA Final Four. As she returns from her ACL tear that kept her out all of last season, she will be looking to show the world she hasn't lost a step.

The 21-year-old got off to an encouraging start on Monday, scoring 21 points in 25 minutes in a blowout defeat of UNLV.

Watkins has been a largely unstoppable scorer and an underappreciated defender in her time as USC's top star. She has averaged over 23 points in both seasons she played, while also averaging over two steals and nearly two blocks a game in that same span.

It is a two-way impact that is incredibly hard to come by. Whether you are the one guarding her or being guarded by her, there is a lot to fear as Watkins steps back on the court in potentially her last ride at USC.

If you can think of an award for best player in women's college basketball, Sarah Strong's name is already on it. Until someone takes it from her, the crown for best player in the NCAA is worn by the star in Storrs.

There already isn't much on the court that Strong cannot do. Now a year removed from the official end of the Paige Bueckers-Azzi Fudd era, the word of the offseason has been assertiveness for Strong—both on the court and as a team leader.

Even with the 20-year-old coming off such a dominating season on both sides of the ball, she still has room to grow. Scary.

articles.title: A Trade Idea to Land Stephen Curry, Golden State Warriors a Kristaps Porziņģis Replacement
articles.summary: The Golden State Warriors expected Kristaps Porziņģis to man the starting center position through the 2026-27 campaign, but the Latvian big man is still working through health issues that have kept him sidelined.
articles.body:
The Golden State Warriors expected Kristaps Porziņģis to man the starting center position through the 2026-27 campaign, but the Latvian big man is still working through health issues that have kept him sidelined.

It's a significant loss, given that Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody are also out for extended periods with knee injuries. Despite three of the Warriors' five highest-paid players being unavailable, the team has reeled off a five-game win streak.

Perhaps it's time for the team to take proactive steps to replace Porziņģis with a shot-blocking veteran center with NBA Finals experience, in a theoretical trade with the Milwaukee Bucks.

*The question remains whether or not Porziņģis returns.

Moody ruptured his left patellar tendon in late March and may be available as early as December or January. But Turner is available immediately.

The teams have no signing restrictions; Golden State can aggregate the two outgoing players to absorb Turner (Sims is on a minimum contract).

Turner, a 6'11" center-forward, is languishing on the post-Giannis-Antetokounmpo Bucks (1-7). His numbers have fallen to a career-low 8.5 points and 5.6 rebounds per game, while he shoots just 31.6 percent from three.

He's also stuck on one of the league's clearest rebuilds. Place him on a squad with talent like Steph Curry, Draymond Green, and Rookie of the Year candidate Yaxel Lendeborg, and Turner's efficiency should quickly climb. He hit 38.3 percent from three last season and was a significant part of the Indiana Pacers' run to the 2024-25 NBA Finals.

Sims, 28, is insurance at the same position, helping the Warriors double up on available size. The cost is second-round considerations, an absent Porziņģis, and letting Moody go. Others like De'Anthony Melton, Brandin Podziemski, and Brandon Williams have contributed well at guard for the Warriors.

The added cost is the financial commitment to Turner, whose contract includes a $29.1 million player option before the 2028-29 season. Porziņģis has a $20 million player option for next year, with just $3 million guaranteed.

Turner has never been a dominant rebounder, but he's averaging 2.8 blocks per game, which would help improve the Warriors' rim protection. The franchise is already limited by a $221.7 million second-apron hard cap—the deal for Turner and Sims lowers overall salary by $3.6 million.

The Bucks were seeking multiple second-round picks for Sims before the season. The Warriors give their 2030 second—which may go to the Dallas Mavericks; if so, Milwaukee gets a 2032 second in the 31-50 range, with 51-60 already obligated to the Memphis Grizzlies—and a 2033 second, along with cash, to offset the $3 million on Porziņģis' contract next year.

Update: Jake Fischer 's sourcing is skeptical that the Warriors would take on Turner's long-term deal.

The Bucks signed Turner last year to complement Antetokounmpo, who is now with the Heat. A key return from Miami was Kel'el Ware, who should start for Milwaukee through this transition year.

Turner carries a heavy contract and is struggling with his shot. If the Warriors are willing to take him on now, by all means. Moody is a talented player once healthy. The Bucks can waive Porziņģis once the trade is finalized, eating the $3 million guaranteed on his deal next season.

The franchise saves $40.6 million in future seasons ($11.5 million and $29.1 million), while adding a couple of second-rounders and $3 million in cash. Sims isn't in head coach Taylor Jenkins' rotation.

While the Bucks can use their $25.5 million Antetokounmpo trade exception to take on Porziņģis, Moody would need to come out of a new one generated for Turner. It would last longer (a full year), but Milwaukee is better off swapping players directly and saving the larger Antetokounmpo exception that expires July 6.

Email Eric Pincus at eric.pincus@gmail.com and follow him on X @EricPincus .

articles.title: Bryce James' Box Score Stats, Highlights from Arizona's Win vs. Cal Poly
articles.summary: Bryce James scored the first points of his college career on Thursday night in Arizona's 104-84 win over Cal Poly.
articles.body:
Bryce James scored the first points of his college career on Thursday night in Arizona's 104-84 win over Cal Poly.

The 19-year-old put up five points in 17 minutes in his second start for the Wildcats.

James, the youngest son of LeBron James, made his college debut on Monday. He played just six minutes and missed all three of his field-goal attempts in Arizona's 84-75 loss to No. 22 UCLA.

Thursday night's matchup against Cal Poly provided James with more runway to get his feet wet as he continues to acclimate himself to college basketball. His first bucket came on a catch-and-shoot three early in the first half.

James was part of the 2025 recruiting class and opted to redshirt during his true freshman season. Head coach Tommy Lloyd explained in February the move was part of a "long play" to give James a proper development window that maximizes his ability.

"The redshirting decision was just a long play, to give Bryce the most options in his career as his career unfolds," Lloyd said. "I have real strong belief that Bryce will be a contributor at Arizona in the near future. He's really shown a lot of progress, not only learning our system but just physically maturing."

There is still plenty of room for James to grow, and he will be doing it in a high-profile environment. Arizona entered the season ranked No. 5 in the AP Top 25 preseason poll.

Next up for James and the Wildcats will be a home game against Northern Arizona on Tuesday.

articles.title: Woke 3.0 is off to a hot start as singer waves Pride flag while performing national anthem during NBA game
articles.summary: A singer waved a small Pride flag while performing the national anthem during Golden State Warriors Pride Night, sparking fierce backlash online.
articles.body: What a week for the left. When you're hot, you're hot! First, they absolutely wiped the floor with Republicans in the midterm elections. Just a bloodbath. I'm pretty sure Democrats now own every single congressional seat known to man, along with a few others we don't even know exist. None of it was great, and it somehow got worse. That's right. It was a blue tsunami on Tuesday, and a red stock market on Thursday. And I mean a reeeeeeeeeeeed stock market. WNBA FINALS TEAMS END SEASON WITH ONE FINAL NATIONAL ANTHEM SNUB AS DREAM, VALKYRIES LEAVE COURT Last night, we saw all the different colors on display our in San Francisco, where a gay man not only sang the national anthem before the Golden State Warriors game, but he also waved a tiny Pride flag during the song. A tiny rainbow flag. During the national anthem. During the actual national anthem. You wanna talk about disrespectful. This makes the WNBA nonsense from last month look like child's play. Woke 3.0 is off to a BLAZING start: This was a step too far, even for the insufferable NBA It's just horrible. It's so embarrassing, and pathetic, and — again — disrespectful. Why? Why do this? Yes, it was "Pride Night" at Oracle Arena because every team has to have a Pride Night. Why? I don't know, but they do. I get it. That's fine. But "Pride Night" doesn't give you a hall pass to do whatever you want during our country's national anthem. Feel like that's off-limits to anything and everything. There's a right way to do it, and a wrong way to do it. No in between. Waving a Pride flag while singing it is the wrong way to do it. Plain and simple. Even the players were stunned by it. Look at them! They can't hold back their laughter. I'm sure Steve Kerr loved it. He's probably still giddy over Tuesday's election results. While Woke 3.0 is very clearly here, sanity still prevailed online, where this gay anthem singer was absolutely crushed for pulling this move: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Why is so difficult to just ... act normal? I don't get it? Just act right. It's not asking a lot. Really, it's not. It's asking that you don't wave your tiny Pride flag during the national anthem, and smirk about it like you're taking some big stand. You're not taking a big stand. You look like an idiot. We're all mocking you. articles.title: Las bestiales cifras que confirman a Doncic como uno de los mejores anotadores de la historia
articles.standfirst: Muchas de las estadísticas del base de los Lakers sólo son comparables a las de Wilt Chamberlain y Michael Jordan
articles.summary: Muchas de las estadísticas del base de los Lakers sólo son comparables a las de Wilt Chamberlain y Michael Jordan
articles.body: "Luka es uno de los mejores anotadores que han jugado a este deporte, si no el mejor", dijo Giannis Antetokounmpo después de que el base de los Lakers les metiera 42 puntos. "¿En este momento?", preguntó un periodista. Y la respuesta del griego fue contundente: "No, en este momento, no. ¡De todos los tiempos! Creo que algunas personas tienen miedo de decirlo, pero él tiene que estar ahí arriba". Los datos no dan la razón a la estrella de los Heat porque han existido jugadores como Wilt Chamberlain y Michael Jordan, pero los registros anotadores de Doncic andan a la zaga. Ahí van. En lo que va de temporada, Doncic ha alcanzado los 40 puntos en cinco de sus ocho encuentros: 52 a los Jazz, 41 a los Blazers, 45 a los Raptors, los mencionados 42 a los Heat y 40 a los Kings. Los tres últimos han sido de manera consecutiva. Su mayor cantidad de partidos en una temporada llegando a esa cifra son 16, conseguidos en la última. Ahora, sin LeBron James en el equipo, como referencia absoluta, va camino de pulverizar esa marca. Doncic acumula 308 puntos en los ocho primeros partidos de la temporada. No se veía algo así desde la campaña 88-89, cuando Michael Jordan se quedó en 303 con los Bulls. El del base esloveno es el mejor inicio anotador desde los tiempos de Wilt Chamberlain, que posee las tres mejores marcas llegando incluso a unos bestiales 418 puntos en el curso 62-63. De mantener su actual media anotadora, algo que se antoja muy complicado, los 38,50 puntos de Doncic en el presente ejercicio serían el tercer mejor registro en la historia. Sólo Chamberlain cerró una temporada con mejor promedio. Lo hizo en dos ocasiones: 50,36 puntos en la 61-62 y 44,83 en la siguiente. La cuarta y la quinta mejor marca también son del legendario pívot. Después vendría una de Jordan. Con su sensacional arranque de campaña, el base de los Lakers ha elevado a 29,37 puntos el promedio de toda su carrera. Eso le sitúa en el tercer puesto en la historia de la NBA. Por delante, los dos clásicos: Jordan se retiró con 30,12 y Chamberlain, con 30,07. Después de las tres últimas actuaciones pasando de los 40 puntos, Doncic acumula ya 67 partidos alcanzando la cuarentena de los 522 que ha disputado en la NBA. Eso significa que llega a esa barrera en el 12,6% de ellos. De nuevo, sólo Chamberlain y Jordan mejoran esa marca. El primero lo hizo en más de una cuarta parte de los encuentros que jugó: 25,9% (271 de 1.045). El segundo, en el 16,1% (173/1.072). Con su último partido, Doncic cumplió los 100 con los Lakers. En ellos ha acumulado 3.240 puntos, que serían la tercera mejor cifra en el primer centenar de partidos con una franquicia. Chamberlain, cómo no, le supera. Metió 3.748 en sus primeros 100 partidos con los Warriors y 3.271 con los Sixers. La media de 32,40 puntos que arrojan esos 100 partidos con los Lakers es la mejor en la historia de la franquicia. Y hablamos de un equipo por el que han pasado algunos de los grandes mitos de la NBA: Elgin Baylor (27,4), Shaquille O'Neal (27,0), Jerry West (27,0), LeBron James (25,9), Kobe Bryant (25,0)... A Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, que bajó sus prestaciones en las últimas temporadas de su carrera, le saca más de 10 puntos de media (22,1).

articles.title: Steph Curry on facing Klay Thompson: 'Every time we play against him it's one closer to the end'
articles.summary: Curry put up 29 points as the Warriors topped the Heat for their sixth straight win.
articles.body:
Thursday was one of those vintage Stephen Curry nights as he dropped 29 points during the Golden State Warriors' 120-100 win over the Miami Heat .

Curry ended the first half 2-for-10 from the field before erupting in the second half, which included hitting six 3-pointers while coming a point shy of a fourth-straight game with 30 points.

With those half dozen 3-pointers, Curry became the first player in NBA history with four consecutive games of making at least five 3-pointers at age 38 or older and he also passed Oscar Robertson for 17th on the all-time scoring list.

The Warriors have now won six games in a row after dropping their first three of the season.

It was also a special night at Chase Center as Curry's former "Splash Brother," Klay Thompson, was in the building.

Before Curry got the win on the court, he had already beaten his former teammate off the court and was ready to collect after his alma mater, Davidson, beat Thompson's, Washington State,, on Monday night.

"We got the dub," a smiling Curry said afterward, "so there was healthy monetary value to that."

Thompson, a day after hitting a game-winning 3-pointer to finish with 30 points during a Heat overtime win over the Los Angeles Clippers, cooled off on Thursday night. He finished with 11 points after going 3-for-10 from the field and 2-for-7 from 3-point range.

The two were involved in several plays together that were surely discussed afterward between the friends. First, Thompson got a block on Curry's opening quarter layup attempt.

Later, Thompson fouled Curry, and after the whistle Curry threw up a one-handed 3-pointer.

"It's still surreal playing against him, it's always going to be that way because we've gone through so many battles together," Curry said.

It's been over two years since Thompson left Golden State and joined the Dallas Mavericks, ending the "Splash Brothers" partnership. With Thompson 36 years old and Curry 38, both know that time is running out and they appreciate these opportunities as they come.

"It was fun. It was really fun. He's still super crafty still to this day," Thompson said. "It felt good to block his shot, he had an incredible night. What Steph is doing, I got to see it every night and it became normal, but to see it as an opponent it was incredible, especially that he's nearing 40 and he moves like a young athlete. It's all the respect in the world for him. He deserves all the accolades and adulation and money. He's just 1 of 1 and the game is going to miss him when he does hang it up."

"It's definitely surreal, but it's also a blessing we're still playing," Curry told NBA TV . "Every time we play against him it's one closer to the end. Just trying to appreciate it."

articles.title: Giannis Antetokounmpo 'didn't want to be the bad guy' and ask for trade from Bucks, says Doc Rivers
articles.summary: Antetokounmpo was eventually dealt in June to the Miami Heat.
articles.body:
Giannis Antetokounmpo did not want to be the "bad guy" and ask for a trade, which is why he kept "yo-yoing" about his future with the Milwaukee Bucks, according to Doc Rivers.

The former Bucks head coach was on " The Bill Simmons Podcast " this week and said Antetokounmpo did not want to publicly ask to be moved — he wanted general manager Jon Horst and owner Wes Edens to be the reasons why the two-time MVP was dealt.

"Giannis wanted out, but he was a Buck. And he didn't want to be the bad guy," Rivers said . "He wanted Jon and Wes and those guys to say, 'We're trading you,' instead of him asking for a trade. To me, that was the game that was being played."

As his time appeared to be coming to an end in Milwaukee and with his future hanging over the franchise last season, Antetokounmpo said multiple times that he would "never" ask out.

"There will never be a chance, and there will never be a moment that I will come out and say, 'I want a trade,'" Antetokounmpo told The Athletic in January.

ESPN's Shams Charania reported that Antetokounmpo's camp had told the team since May 2025 that he felt it was best the two sides part ways.

The Antetokounmpo trade drama finally ended in June when he was dealt to the Miami Heat .

Rivers also spoke about how difficult it was to coach Antetokounmpo when the two worked together for parts of three seasons with the Bucks.

"He's not easy. He plays at this crazy downhill pace. He's really a difficult guy," Rivers said. "He has this great passing ability, but he doesn't necessarily have super IQ at the same time. It's really a strange thing. He really has one way. Every play he wants to force it. I wished he learned how to execute better.

"The thing he needs to still learn is the value of execution. How important it is when you're in practice and in shootaround to lock in on execution. Now he has a coach who's as good as there is in execution."

While Antetokounmpo is off to a strong start through nine games by averaging 27.3 points, 12.7 rebounds and 5.6 assists per night, the Heat are 3-6. The Bucks, meanwhile, are 1-9 and enter Friday's game against the Toronto Raptors losers of four in a row.

articles.title: Clippers Eyed as NBA Trade 'Sellers' by Insiders in New Rumors amid Slow Start
articles.summary: Amid a 1-7 start that has them tied for the worst record in the NBA, the Los Angeles Clippers have emerged as a potential seller as teams begin to think about moves they want to make.
articles.body:
Amid a 1-7 start that has them tied for the worst record in the NBA, the Los Angeles Clippers have emerged as a potential seller as teams begin to think about moves they want to make.

Per ESPN's Tim MacMahon , multiple scouts and league executives have cited the Clippers as "likely sellers" given their current situation.

The Clippers have four players on expiring contracts who would likely have at least some level appeal to playoff contenders. That group includes Max Strus, Kris Dunn, Derrick Jones Jr. and Brook Lopez.

Rui Hachimura is another potential pending free agent with a $14 million team option for 2027-28.

After trading Ivica Zubac prior to the trade deadline last season and Kawhi Leonard over the summer, the Clippers signaled they were turning the page on the previous era and wanted to look toward the future.

The Clippers' future is complicated due to the discipline levied by the NBA due to salary-cap circumvention involving endorsement deals given to Leonard.

Their punishment included forfeiting five first-round draft picks from 2029 to '33. Their 2027 and 2028 first-round selections are tied up in swap deals, so they won't control their own top pick again until 2034.

The Leonard trade did help mitigate some of the sting because the Clippers acquired unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and '33 from the Toronto Raptors in the deal.

It will be interesting to see how the Clippers go about using those picks — either holding onto them, or trying to package them for help — because their current roster has not shown the ability to compete in the Western Conference.

Los Angeles has lost seven straight games after beating the Sacramento Kings in the season opener. The Clippers rank 21st in net rating and are one of five teams with just one victory so far in 2026-27.

articles.title: Forget the schedule, Jalen Brunson has another theory to explain the NBA injury crisis
articles.summary: Almost every team in the NBA has been hit by injuries this season. We are less than a month into the new campaign, and several big names have already been si...
articles.body:
Almost every team in the NBA has been hit by injuries this season.

We are less than a month into the new campaign, and several big names have already been sidelined due to one issue or another. There are fears that the list could grow in the coming weeks and months.

Many feel the schedule is the reason why, but Jalen Brunson has a different theory.

Jalen Brunson says the NBA's injury crisis could be down to 'style of play'

It has been a real shame to see several fantastic players miss games due to injuries this season.

From Anthony Edwards and Ja Morant to Paolo Banchero and Kawhi Leonard, many are currently sidelined, causing their respective teams to be significantly weaker.

Several theories have been going around – from the gruelling schedule to a lack of preparation in pre-season practice sessions.

But Jalen Brunson thinks it may actually be down to the style of play most coaches employ in the NBA in today's game.

When told that 16-20 per cent of the league is on the injury report, Brunson said on the Roommates Show : "I just feel like it's a lot.

"Is the schedule asking too much of the players? No! I mean, the schedule is the schedule. It's been that way for – we've been playing 82 games for, I don't know how many years – like decades.

"But it's obviously unfortunate things happen, but yeah, I don't think it's the scheduling part. I think maybe it's like the style of play. We're playing fast-paced basketball."

The intensity involved in almost every team sport in the world has gone up in recent years, and it is showing no signs of slowing down.

That has definitely made games more interesting, but it has to be said that the physical burden on players has gone up as well. That increases the risk of injuries, which we are all seeing right now.
